summary: Adds new assertion values for the Resource Priority Header claim and a new SIP Priority Header claim in PASSporT, to protect the psap-callback value. This supports the security of emergency services networks for call origination and callback.

eli5.summary: Emergency calls get a signed stamp saying this is a priority call back from the emergency center, so it can not be faked.

questions: what is the sph claim in passport
what is esnet in resource priority header
subtitle: Signed assertions that an emergency call or a PSAP callback really has the priority it claims.

tldr.problem: Priority markings on emergency calls and PSAP callbacks in the SIP Resource-Priority and Priority header fields could be compromised and misused, for example during congestion.
tldr.mechanism: New "esnet.x" values for the "rph" claim and a new "sph" claim let the authorized signer cryptographically sign those header values in a PASSporT.
tldr.outcome: A receiver, even in another network domain, can verify the priority values were not spoofed. The scope is emergency services only.

facts.label: IANA
facts.value: Adds sph to the JSON Web Token Claims registry

today: RFC 9027 is a Proposed Standard, published in June 2021. It is not obsoleted or updated by any other RFC in the unit metadata.

sections.title: Protecting Emergency Priority Markings
sections.content:
RFC 8443 extended the PASSporT token of RFC 8225 so a party can sign the values in the SIP Resource-Priority header field. This document adds new auth values for the rph claim and a new claim, sph, for the SIP Priority header field, for emergency call origination and callback.

The motivation is that compromising these header fields could lead to misuse of network resources, such as during congestion, and affect the handling of Public Safety Answering Point (PSAP) callbacks. A signed header lets a receiver, including one in another network domain, act on it with confidence that it was not spoofed.

The claims are meant for environments where the signer of the headers can be verified as authoritative. Their use for emergency services is introduced elsewhere and is otherwise out of scope here.
sections.eli5: If anyone could claim a call was an emergency, they could cut in line. A signature proves the claim came from someone allowed to make it.

sections.title: The esnet Values for the rph Claim
sections.content:
The document lets the SIP Resource-Priority namespace for local emergency communications, written esnet.x (RFC 7135), be signed. At the time of writing, x is between 0 and 4 inclusive, and may be extended later. The value should exactly match the Resource-Priority header field of the call.

For a call to emergency services, the orig claim MUST be the calling party number. The dest claim MUST be a country- or region-specific dial string (such as 911 or 112) or urn:service:sos.

For a callback, the orig claim MUST be the PSAP telephone number, and dest MUST be the number of the original caller being called back.

The signature is generated per RFC 8225 using the full form of PASSporT. The certificate used must have authority over the namespace of the rph claim, with only one authority per claim. If intermediaries add or drop r-values, they must generate a new rph identity header and sign it with their own authority.
sections.eli5: The stamp says which emergency level the call has. For a normal emergency call it names the caller. For a callback it names the emergency center.

sections.title: The sph Claim
sections.content:
RFC 7090 allows the SIP Priority header field to be psap-callback for emergency callbacks. Some SIP networks act on that value, so its authoritative use needs protection.

The new sph claim is optional. It MUST only be used with an auth value of esnet.x indicating an authorized emergency callback, and corresponds to a Priority header field of psap-callback. The value should only be psap-callback and MUST match the header. Any other value is a PASSporT validation failure.

The signer is assumed to be authoritative for both header fields in an emergency callback. The document is not a general mechanism for protecting the SIP Priority header, which could be future work.
sections.eli5: A second stamp on the callback says it is a callback from the emergency center. If the stamp says anything else, the check fails.

sections.title: Claim Order and Compact Form
sections.content:
The claim keys MUST follow the deterministic JSON serialization rules in Section 9 of RFC 8225, in lexicographic order. In the payload they appear as dest, iat, orig, rph, sph.

The compact form of PASSporT is not specified in this document and is not recommended for rph PASSporTs.
sections.eli5: The parts of the stamp must always be written in the same alphabetical order, so the signature check works the same everywhere.

sections.title: IANA and Security
sections.content:
The document asks IANA to add one claim to the JSON Web Token Claims registry (RFC 7519): name sph, description SIP Priority header field, change controller IESG.

For security, the considerations in RFC 8224, RFC 8225 and RFC 8443 apply. The document adds no further security text.
sections.eli5: The new stamp name gets written in the official list of names. The old safety rules still apply.
